The first thing my father taught me to repair was a drawer.

Not a clock, not a bicycle, nothing that rewarded competence by moving. Just a kitchen drawer that stuck every winter and opened too freely in summer, spilling birthday candles and rubber bands onto the floor.

“Wood remembers being a tree,” he said.

This was not a useful explanation. I was nine and wanted instructions.

He turned the drawer upside down on the table. There were pale tracks along its sides where the wood had rubbed itself smooth.

“Here.”

He gave me a stub of candle.

I waxed the runners. We put the drawer back. It opened.

For several days I found reasons to retrieve things nobody needed.

***

Thirty years later, after his funeral, I went through his house with a yellow legal pad.

The pad was my sister’s idea.

Three columns: KEEP, DONATE, DISCARD.

“You need a system,” she said over the phone.

She had children, a bad knee, and a job that required her to use the phrase “capacity planning.” She would come on Saturday. Until then I had the system.

I began with the kitchen.

Six mugs. Four ordinary, one commemorating a bank that no longer existed, one with a handle he had repaired using a small metal bracket and two screws.

I held the repaired mug over the DISCARD column.

He had owned a drill bit fine enough to make those holes. Somewhere in the house, I would have to find it and decide what to do with that, too.

I put the mug back.

***

In the garage, jars of screws stood beneath a shelf of useful-looking pieces of wood.

My father labeled everything, but his labels anticipated a reader who already knew what he meant.

GOOD WIRE.

OTHER HINGES.

DO NOT USE.

The last was on a biscuit tin containing what appeared to be perfectly usable bolts. I did not trust them.

There was a cardboard box marked BITS FROM THINGS.

Inside were a brass wheel, a blue plastic lever, three springs, and the little door from a toy ambulance I had owned.

I remembered the ambulance but not losing the door. I remembered making its siren noise under the dining table while my parents tried to listen to the weather forecast.

He must have found the door afterward. Perhaps he had meant to fix it that evening.

I sat on his work stool. One leg was shorter than the others, and he had corrected this with a folded square of sandpaper taped around the foot.

Even his repairs needed repairs.

***

At noon, the woman next door knocked.

She carried soup in a saucepan.

“I didn’t know what you’d have unpacked,” she said.

“I’m packing.”

“Yes, of course.”

Her name was Mrs. Alvarez. She had lived beside him for eleven years. I knew her mostly as a voice asking him, during our telephone calls, whether he wanted anything from the shops.

She looked past me toward the hall.

“He fixed my gate in March.”

“He liked fixing things.”

“He didn’t like my gate.”

That surprised a laugh out of me.

“He said it had been hung by an optimist.”

We ate soup at the kitchen table. Mrs. Alvarez told me about the gate, her grandson’s bicycle, a lamp with an unreliable switch.

Then she said, “He talked about you.”

I looked down at my spoon.

“He said you make maps.”

“I work on routing software.”

“Yes,” she said. “He wasn’t sure what to call it.”

I had explained my work to him several times, usually while doing something else. He asked questions about delivery vans. I corrected him: our largest customers operated freight networks.

Now I wished I had let us talk about vans.

***

That afternoon I found his notebook.

Most pages contained measurements.

Window, back room: 43⅝.

Alvarez gate: lift ¼.

There were shopping lists and telephone numbers. Near the middle, on a page otherwise blank, he had written:

Ask about the maps.

I read it standing up.

Then I sat down.

I could picture him writing it before one of our Sunday calls, putting the notebook beside the telephone. I could not remember whether he had asked.

***

When my sister arrived, she found the legal pad on the table.

Under KEEP I had written:

notebook  
blue bowl  
photographs  
mug?

The other columns were empty.

“You’ve been busy,” she said.

“I made a start.”

She picked up the mug and examined its bracket.

“God, Dad.”

She put it down carefully.

We worked together through the afternoon. She was better at throwing things away, though she quietly pocketed a cheap vegetable peeler I had already put in the rubbish.

At five, the kitchen drawer stuck.

She pulled harder.

“Lift the left side,” I said.

It opened with a wooden complaint.

We took it out and laid it upside down on the table. My sister found the birthday candles. I rubbed one along the runners while she held the drawer steady.

There was a new scrape near the back. We looked for its cause and found a screw projecting from the cabinet.

She fetched a screwdriver from the garage.

We were keeping those.

***

The house sold in November.

Before we handed over the keys, I opened the kitchen drawer once more. It slid easily, empty now except for a stub of yellow candle.

I left that in the corner.

Then I went back, took it out, and put it with the spare keys and appliance manuals, where somebody might actually find it.
